en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, Nissaggiyakaṇḍa (The Chapter on Forfeiture for Nuns)
The Chapter on Robes 12.
The Training Rule on Light Outer Garments.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and skilled in delivering a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having put on expensive linen cloth during the heat of the day, approached the bhikkhunī Thullanandā; having approached, he paid homage to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā and sat down to one side.
As King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting there to one side, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the bhikkhunī Thullanandā’s discourse on the Dhamma, said this to her:
“Venerable lady, please say whatever you require.”
“If you wish to give me anything, Great King, give me this linen cloth.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having given the linen cloth to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, rose from his seat, paid homage to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, and keeping her to his right, departed.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“These bhikkhunīs have great desires and are discontented.
How can they request linen cloth from the king?
The bhikkhunīs heard those people complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the noble lady Thullanandā request linen cloth from the king? ... [They asked:
"Is it true, monks, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā requests linen cloth from the king?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:
“… How indeed, monks, can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā request linen cloth from a king?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:

‘When a bhikkhunī is having a light cloak made, it should be made at most two-and-a-half kaṃsas in weight. If she should have it made beyond that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.’”
A light cloak means any cloak used during the hot season.
"Causing to be paid" means...
"For one who makes it known.
"It may be bartered for up to two and a half kaṁsas" means it may be bartered for something worth ten kārṣāpaṇas.
"If he should cause it to be procured beyond that" means:
if he requests more than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act;
with the acquisition [of the item], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And thus, monks, it should be relinquished:
…pe…
“Venerable ladies, this light cloak of mine, purchased for no more than two and a half kaṁsas, is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “She should give it back” …pe… “They should give it back” …pe…
“I give it to the noble lady.

If she causes [the robe] to be procured while perceiving it to be more than two and a half kaṁsas when it is more than two and a half kaṁsas, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If she causes it to be procured while being in doubt as to whether it is more than two and a half kaṁsas when it is more than two and a half kaṁsas, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If she causes [a robe] to be sought when it is less than two and a half kaṁsas, but perceives it as such, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is less than two and a half kaṁsas and she perceives it as more, there is an offense of wrongdoing.
If it is less than two and a half kaṁsas and she is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing.
If it is less than two and a half kaṁsas and she perceives it as less,
there is no offense.
There is no offense if she causes [the robe] to be procured up to the limit of two and a half kaṁsas.
If she causes [it] to be procured for no more than two and a half kaṃsas,
[from] relatives or those who have invited her;
If, for the sake of another,
one causes something of little value to be purchased with one's own wealth by someone desiring to purchase something of great value;
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-offender.
The twelfth training rule is concluded.
(Second) Chapter on Bowls 10.
The Training Rule on What is Consumed:
Venerable ladies, the thirty rules of expiation involving forfeiture have been recited.
In this matter, friends, I ask you:
"Are you pure in this?
A second time I ask: [the same].
“Are you pure in this matter?
For a third time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
"Venerable ladies, this matter is pure; therefore, you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The section on offenses entailing relinquishment in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.
